preserved (visible aerated lung rim separates the opacity from the heart) or obscured (opacity merges with/blends into the heart contour).", "Apply the silhouette sign: A preserved border indicates the lesion is not in direct contact with the mediastinal pleura/pericardium (e.g., peripheral lung, posterior lower lobe), whereas an obscured border indicates direct anatomical contact (e.g., middle lobe, lingula, or anterior segment of the lower lobe)."]}, {"category": "comparison", "trigger": "When evaluating serial chest X-rays to determine the progression or resolution of extra-alveolar air (pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema).", "steps": ["Inspect the initial image for vertical lucent streaks paralleling the mediastinal structures (especially the left heart border and aorta) and radiolucent striations within the soft tissues of the neck, axillae, or chest wall.", "Examine the follow-up image specifically at the mediastinal contours and soft tissue planes to verify if these lucencies have disappeared and normal anatomical interfaces have been restored.", "Distinguish complete resolution (absence of all abnormal lucencies in both compartments) from partial Based on the chest X-ray findings, which statement best describes the location and impact of the mediastinal mass on surrounding structures in the 11-year-old boy's chest?  
A) The mediastinal mass is located primarily on the left side, causing significant displacement of the trachea to the right.  
B) The mediastinal mass is located primarily on the right side, causing displacement of the trachea to the left.  
C) The mediastinal mass is located centrally, causing equal displacement of the trachea to both sides.  
D) The mediastinal mass is located on the right side and causes compression of the left main bronchus.  
E) The mediastinal mass is located on the left side and does not cause any tracheal displacement.  
F) The mediastinal mass is located centrally but does not affect the trachea.
